channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: New smartphone tool could help young people seek support for eating disorders earlier
item.description: Researchers have found that a smartphone-friendly digital tool designed to encourage help-seeking among young people with eating disorders is both feasible and acceptable, paving the way for a larger clinical trial.

item.title: Researchers urge significant 'peacetime' investment in contact tracing apps and digital public health tools
item.description: Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, university researchers have detailed how public health agencies across the world can be better prepared for the next epidemic through effective deployment of Bluetooth contact tracing apps and related digital public health tools.

item.title: Discovery points to new approach for treating diabetes—no insulin required
item.description: Researchers at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown way the body's muscles absorb glucose from the blood—without insulin.

item.title: Brain stacking: An expert weighs in on whether this TikTok trend can really boost your brainpower
item.description: Brain stacking is a new TikTok trend dedicated to making time for activities that engage our mind, such as reading or doing puzzles.

item.title: Newly discovered mechanism may help ovarian cancer cells silence tumor-suppressor genes
item.description: Researchers at Umeå University have discovered how chemical marks on RNA control a DNA methylation enzyme and contribute to the silencing of tumor-suppressor genes in ovarian cancer cells. The findings provide new insights into the disease and may, in the long term, contribute to the development of new treatment strategies for high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

item.title: Screen time and smart device usage reflected in adolescent brain structures involved in attention, memory and learning
item.description: According to a recent Finnish study, leisure-time screen time, total physical activity and physical fitness are reflected in the brain structures of young people in various ways. Adolescents who spent a lot of time on screens and smart devices had a smaller volume of gray matter in the medial temporal lobe related to memory and learning than others. The paper is published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports.

item.title: Injectable hydrogel material shows promise for regenerating damaged tissue
item.description: A biomedical engineer at the University of Houston has developed an injectable peptide hydrogel—about the consistency of hand sanitizer—that stimulates new blood vessel growth while providing structural support for healing tissue. The discovery, published in Science Advances by Vivek Kumar, associate professor of biomedical engineering at UH, and colleagues, offers a customizable blueprint for regenerative medicine.

item.title: What is 'intergenerational trauma'? A social worker explains how one generation's experiences can affect descendants
item.description: Throughout history, millions of people have experienced widespread violence, persecution and loss. During the Holocaust, 6 million Jewish people were murdered. Beginning in 1619 and through the mid-1800s, 12.5 million African people were forced onto ships during the trans-Atlantic slave trade. These are just two examples of many that have affected communities in ways that last long after the initial experiences.

item.title: An experimental treatment improves the cognitive ability and gut microbiota of mice with fragile X syndrome
item.description: Ongoing treatment with a drug that inhibits the endocannabinoid system peripherally improves memory deficits, reduces synaptic alterations, mitigates gut microbiota dysbiosis and restores intestinal barrier integrity markers in fragile X syndrome mouse models. This experimental approach opens the door to studying a potential therapy to improve the cognitive ability of people who have the syndrome and underscores the role that alterations to the microbiota–gut–brain axis may play in intellectual disability.

item.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes therapies show great promise—but treatment is only effective if people can access it
item.description: In 2026, over 830 million people worldwide are estimated to live with diabetes—more than ever before.

item.title: AI in medicine and biology: Researchers call for a multilayered security architecture
item.description: Artificial intelligence is now capable not only of analyzing biological data but also of designing new DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. To lay the groundwork for responsible innovation, an international and interdisciplinary research team led by University Medical Center Mainz proposes a multi-tiered security architecture for the use of generative AI in biology. The publication was published in the journal Nature Communications.

item.title: Commonly mutated gene could be a therapeutic target in sarcoma
item.description: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have discovered that sarcomas lacking the ATRX gene tend to be more aggressive and may be particularly vulnerable to a class of targeted therapies known as TEAD inhibitors. The findings identify ATRX loss as both a marker of poor prognosis and a potential therapeutic target.

item.title: The Harry Potter soundtrack helps researchers test how the brain differentiates speech and background music
item.description: When speech and music overlap or occur in rapid succession, listeners can recognize both almost instantaneously. Researchers have wanted to understand why this happens for a while. Now, a new study, published in Science Advances, corroborates previous findings that suggest the brain's auditory cortex differentiates between speech and music using patterns that describe how acoustic energy changes over time and across frequencies. The new study suggests these processes are sufficient to do the job under normal listening conditions—which, in this study, involve the Harry Potter soundtrack.

item.title: EU officials call for 'swift and sustained' action on antimicrobial resistance
item.description: European health officials are calling for urgent action as a series of new reports shows a mixed picture on antibiotic consumption and antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

item.title: Ultrasound imaging without the goop: A gel-free patch shows promise
item.description: Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology's Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care project (SMART WITEC) have developed a dry and stretchy material that could eliminate the need for a wet and sticky gel in ultrasound imaging.

item.title: Scientists find the brain's blueprint for spoken words
item.description: A new discovery by scientists at UC San Francisco rewrites our understanding of how the human brain processes speech, challenging the century-old view that understanding and producing speech are handled by separate systems. It also resolves a longstanding paradox: Why can injury to a brain region that is critical for speech comprehension also impair the ability to produce words?

item.title: Low back pain patients carry similar abdominal muscle mass to others, study finds
item.description: People with low back pain have about the same amount of abdominal muscle as people without it, but a lower ratio of abdominal muscle to fat, according to a new study published Nov. 19 in the journal PLOS Digital Health by Kathryn Marusich of Stanford University, U.S., and colleagues.

item.title: Army blast in Iowa could spread toxic lead dust up to 100 miles
item.description: The U.S. Army plans to blow up unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa on Friday, a blast that could carry toxic lead dust up to 100 miles (161 kilometers).

item.title: A shared molecular weakness in glioblastoma tumor cells may offer a new treatment target
item.description: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a shared molecular trait in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer in adults. It resembles one used by immature cells during brain development and may reveal a target for future treatments.

item.title: Two new 16-week tuberculosis regimens advance in clinical trial
item.description: Tuberculosis remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, causing more than 1 million deaths each year. The development of new therapeutic regimens remains slow, costly and complex, while treatment remains lengthy and patients face the burden of side effects. Accelerating the identification of safer, shorter and more effective treatment options is essential to achieving global TB elimination goals.

item.title: Duran Duran's drummer has retired because of tinnitus—here's why musicians are at higher risk
item.description: After more than 40 years performing with Duran Duran, drummer Roger Taylor has announced he's retiring because of his worsening tinnitus.

item.title: PACER trial evaluates online cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety after chest pain
item.description: Some patients returned to the emergency department with the same chest pain that had brought them in before, even after an evaluation ruled out a heart attack or another emergency. For emergency physician and Regenstrief Institute research scientist Paul I. Musey Jr., M.D., M.S., those repeat visits raised a question: What could emergency departments offer patients who also screened positive for clinically significant anxiety?

item.title: Lingering CAR T cells may be the cause of serious gut complication after myeloma therapy
item.description: Patients with multiple myeloma who developed a serious gastrointestinal side effect after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy had significantly more CAR T cells persisting in their bloodstream, according to new research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

item.title: Mpox cases persist in US, but public awareness remains low
item.description: Four years after a major global outbreak of mpox, the United States continues to see a persistent, low level of cases of the viral disease. But Americans' awareness and knowledge of mpox have changed little over the past couple of years, according to a new nationally representative survey conducted by the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania.

item.title: Little-known protein may help protect spinal disks from aging
item.description: University of Utah researchers have characterized a protein that may help protect spinal disks from age-related damage, pointing to a possible direction for future back pain treatments. Using CRISPR to target ZNF865, also known as BLST, in human cells and mouse and rat models, the interdisciplinary team showed how increasing or decreasing BLST levels affected spinal disk health.

item.title: Smart floss can measure blood sugar and inflammation markers
item.description: While the biological link between oral health and whole-body wellness has long been recognized, medicine has lacked practical tools to monitor both at home. To bridge this gap, an interdisciplinary research team led by The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) has developed an innovative gingival fluid device (GFD) featuring a disposable "Smart Floss" with a microfluidic channel and sensor array built directly inside.

item.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture—here's how food scientists manufacture it
item.description: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

item.title: Infinite scroll and autoplay are fueling a global problem, commission warns
item.description: More than one in 10 people worldwide may be affected by problematic internet use, with researchers warning the economic and social costs could run into billions of dollars each year. In the U.K. alone, this burden has been estimated at £10 billion to £12 billion annually.

item.title: Exercise intensity may influence postexercise cooling
item.description: Athletes and physically active individuals often exercise in hot environments, which can dangerously increase body temperature and cardiovascular strain. Water immersion is a commonly used strategy to cool the body after exercise because water transfers heat more efficiently than air. However, how quickly the body cools down may depend on the type of exercise performed before cooling begins.

item.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
item.description: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.
